A French courtier conceived the painting as an erotic portrait of his mistress and initially offered the commission to the religious painter Gabriel-François Doyen. 

The courtier instructed Doyen to depict the mistress being pushed on a swing by a bishop while positioning the patron below to look up her skirt. 

Horrified by the scandalous and anti-clerical nature of the request, Doyen refused the commission and recommended Jean-Honoré Fragonard instead. 

Fragonard accepted the lucrative private assignment to escape the financial and bureaucratic frustrations of working for the royal arts administration. 

The 4th Marquess of Hertford bought the work at the duc de Morny's 1865 Paris auction for 30,200 francs, later leaving it to Sir Richard Wallace. 

Sir Richard's wife, Lady Wallace, kept the painting in her private bedroom before bequeathing the entire collection to the British nation.

gemini.text:
There is no surviving contemporary documentation recording who commissioned the painting, the original contract, or how much Sandro Botticelli was paid for it. 

The earliest written record of the work dates to 1550, when Giorgio Vasari reported seeing it at the Medici family's country estate, the Villa di Castello. 

Historians believe the classical subject was likely devised by the Medici court poet Agnolo Poliziano, possibly commissioned by Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici. 

Unlike many Renaissance panel paintings that were destroyed during Girolamo Savonarola's "Bonfire of the Vanities" in the 1490s, the work survived largely because it was kept safely outside Florence at the villa. 

Botticelli chose canvas rather than expensive wood paneling because canvas was cheaper, lighter, and practical for large decorative hangings in country villas. 

The painting remained largely overlooked and uncelebrated for nearly three centuries until it was relocated to the Uffizi Gallery in 1815 and revived by nineteenth-century art critics.

The painting shows Venus arriving on the shore of Cyprus or Kithera, born from sea foam and blown by the wind god Zephyr, who carries the nymph Chloris. It was painted on canvas using tempera, a technique that allowed for a delicate transparency, and was unusual at the time since most paintings were on wood panels. The orange trees in the painting are considered an emblem of the Medici family, linking the work to their dynasty. Giorgio Vasari first described the painting in the mid-16th century as part of the Medici collection at the Villa of Castello.
